title: How NOT to Coach; How NOT to Teach
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: Using a youth baseball fielding drill as a negative example, the author argues that coaches could learn from great teachers. In the drill, one player fielded at a time while about ten children idled in the outfield and five coaches stood by. From this she draws principles for instruction: maximize the time all children spend actually doing the thing, give immediate corrective feedback, and execute good activities well. Classroom clips of first- and second-grade teachers show every child getting many responses in a few minutes. The core claim is that high-quality instruction is the high-quality execution of high-quality activities, not just a good activity.
points: Maximize the number of at bats every child gets to read, write and apply learning.
Calling on one student at a time leaves most of the class idle.
Immediate corrective feedback is needed to produce change and growth.
A sound activity can be undermined by poor execution, such as making children wait in line.
Classroom clips show whole-class participation in word chaining.
quotes: We need to maximize the amount of time children are doing the THING, whether it’s reading, writing, throwing, catching, or hitting.
High-quality instruction is not just a high-quality activity. It’s high-quality execution of high-quality activities.

The other four coaches hung out on the sidelines, occasionally retrieving stray balls. The ten kids who were not part of the drill idled in the outfield, chatting with their teammates, and waiting for their turn.

Players were practicing fielding ground balls and throwing to first, two essential baseball skills that are valuable to practice in sequence. But the execution (making the kids wait in line) undermined the drill.
Great teachers give immediate, corrective feedback. At this practice, it was unclear if the players were getting feedback at all–and if they were, it certainly wasn’t immediate.

A less knowledgeable teacher (or one more concerned with classroom management) might take this great activity and reduce its effectiveness by inviting a single student to lead the word-chaining in front of the class, while the rest of the class looks on.
